title: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
events_chronological: At the Marcia Blaine School, Miss Jean Brodie takes charge of a set of ten-year-old girls and tells them she is in her prime.
Miss Brodie teaches the girls about her dead fiance Hugh, about Italian painting and about her own opinions, in place of the syllabus.
Miss Brodie walks the set through the old town and stops them in front of a queue of unemployed men.
The headmistress Miss Mackay tries repeatedly to force Miss Brodie's resignation and can find no grounds for it.
The art master Teddy Lloyd, who has one arm, a wife and six children, kisses Miss Brodie in the art room.
Miss Brodie gives up Teddy Lloyd and takes the singing master Gordon Lowther as her lover instead.
Miss Brodie spends her weekends at Lowther's house on the coast with two of the girls in attendance as chaperones.
Miss Brodie decides that Rose Stanley shall become Teddy Lloyd's lover in her place.
Mary Macgregor, the stupid one everybody blames for everything, leaves the school.
Sandy Stranger rather than Rose becomes Teddy Lloyd's lover, and finds that every portrait he paints of any of the girls comes out looking like Miss Brodie.
Miss Brodie encourages a new girl, Joyce Emily Hammond, to run away and fight in Spain.
Joyce Emily is killed when her train is attacked, having gone to fight for the wrong side.
Gordon Lowther marries the science mistress Miss Lockhart.
Sandy tells Miss Mackay that Miss Brodie is a teacher of fascism, and hands the headmistress the grounds she has wanted for years.
Miss Brodie is forced into retirement and spends the rest of her life trying to work out which girl betrayed her.
Mary Macgregor dies at twenty-three in a hotel fire, running the wrong way along a corridor.
Miss Brodie dies of an internal growth, and Sandy, now a cloistered nun who has written a book on psychology, is asked through the grille what the main influences of her schooldays were.
syuzhet_notes: The narration interrupts the schooldays repeatedly to state and then stage what becomes of the girls, so a pupil's death in a hotel fire and another's life behind a convent grille arrive long before the school years they belong after. Both are shown as scenes, not merely foretold.
fabula_notes: The chronology of the school years is fixed by the girls' ages and by the war the new girl runs off to. The two future scenes are dated by the ages the narration gives.
